To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the gold standard verification approach is more robust to model misspecification and that (2) when verification is at random, estimates of diagnostic accuracy are not biased by verification rate.

(1) latent modeling approaches can be used to estimate diagnostic error in the presence of partial gold standard information, and (2) choosing between models that describe the dependence between tests is easier when the partial gold standard information is used in estimation.

(1) latent modeling approaches to estimating diagnostic error are robust to misspecified dependence structure when a subset of subjects is verified, and (2) choosing between competing latent models for estimating diagnostic error is easier when a subset of the subjects is verified.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of estimating diagnostic accuracy from studies with partial gold standard evaluation.
estimating diagnostic error when a gold standard is not available for all subjects.
estimating the sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic tests when the gold standard is not available on all subjects.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in situations in which a gold standard cannot be obtained, it is possible to obtain more accurate estimates of diagnostic accuracy by incorporating partial gold standard information.
the gold standard information is valuable but not always necessary.

, in the presence of a gold standard, the estimation of diagnostic error is not very sensitive to model choice and that the use of gold standard verification on a subset of the subjects is a reasonable compromise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is often possible to estimate diagnostic error in a setting where gold standard evaluation is not possible for all subjects.

, when gold standard evaluation is not feasible for a large portion of subjects in a diagnostic test evaluation study, a compromise approach is possible that provides more accurate estimates of diagnostic accuracy than models without gold standard verification.
it is possible to estimate the diagnostic accuracy of a set of tests or raters when gold standard evaluation is limited to a small subset of subjects.
